title: Space trip
subject: Science
description: Meet the Sun, Moon, and planets.
lesson: The Sun is our nearest star. Its light and heat help life on Earth.
Earth spins, making day and night. Earth also travels around the Sun.
The Moon travels around Earth. Eight planets travel around the Sun.
tryIt: With a grown-up, use a ball and a flashlight to model day and night. Never look at the Sun.

questions.prompt: What is the Sun?
questions.explanation: The Sun is the star at the center of our solar system.

questions.prompt: Which planet is our home?
questions.explanation: We live on Earth, the third planet from the Sun.

questions.prompt: What causes day and night on Earth?
options: The Moon hiding the Sun every night
questions.explanation: Earth spins. The side facing the Sun has day.

questions.prompt: What does the Moon travel around?
questions.explanation: Our Moon orbits, or travels around, Earth.

questions.prompt: Which planet is famous for its bright rings?
questions.explanation: Saturn has a large, bright ring system made of ice and rock.

questions.prompt: How many planets are in our solar system?
questions.explanation: There are eight planets. Pluto is a dwarf planet.

questions.prompt: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Mercury travels closest to the Sun.

questions.prompt: Which gives Earth light and heat?
questions.explanation: The Sun supplies energy that warms and lights Earth.

title: Cloud detectives
subject: Science
lesson: Weather is what the air is like in a place now: sunny, rainy, windy, or snowy.
Liquid water can become water vapor in the air. Cooling vapor can form tiny droplets in clouds.
Rain and snow bring water back down. A thermometer measures temperature.
tryIt: Draw today’s weather. With a grown-up, compare it with tomorrow’s weather.

questions.prompt: Which tool measures temperature?
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures how hot or cold something is.

questions.prompt: What is evaporation?
questions.explanation: Water can change from a liquid into water vapor in the air.

questions.prompt: Tiny water droplets gather in the sky. What can they form?
questions.explanation: Clouds contain tiny water droplets or ice crystals.

questions.prompt: Which is precipitation?
questions.explanation: Precipitation is water falling from clouds, including rain and snow.

questions.prompt: What is wind?
questions.explanation: Wind is air moving from place to place.

questions.prompt: A puddle shrinks on a warm day. Where can its water go?
questions.explanation: Some liquid water evaporates into water vapor.

questions.prompt: Which tells about weather today?
questions.explanation: Weather describes conditions such as rain, wind, and temperature.

questions.prompt: Water cools below its freezing point. What can liquid water become?
questions.explanation: When liquid water freezes, it becomes solid ice.

title: Animal homes
subject: Science
lesson: A habitat is a place where a living thing gets what it needs.
Animals need food, water, air, and a suitable place to live. Plants need water, light, air, and room to grow.
Living things are connected. Many bees carry pollen between flowers.
tryIt: Watch a plant or an animal without disturbing it. Draw its food, water, and shelter.

questions.prompt: What is a habitat?
options: A place a living thing lives
questions.explanation: A habitat provides conditions and resources a living thing needs.

questions.prompt: What does a plant use sunlight to help make?
questions.explanation: Plants use light energy to help make food.

questions.prompt: Which animal has feathers?
questions.explanation: Birds have feathers. A robin is a bird.

questions.prompt: Which is a living thing?
questions.explanation: An oak tree grows and is a living thing.

questions.prompt: Why might a turtle need a pond?
questions.explanation: Many turtles find food and shelter in or near water. Different species have different needs.

questions.prompt: What can many bees carry between flowers?
questions.explanation: Many bees help pollination by moving pollen between flowers.

questions.prompt: What should you do when you see a wild animal?
questions.explanation: Give wild animals space. Observe without touching or feeding them.

questions.prompt: A food chain shows what?
options: How food energy moves between living things
questions.explanation: A simple food chain might go from grass to a rabbit to a fox.

title: Fossil hunt
subject: Science
description: Look for clues from long ago.
lesson: Fossils are preserved remains or traces of living things from long ago.
A footprint can be a fossil, too. Scientists use fossils as evidence.
Non-bird dinosaurs lived long before humans. Birds are living dinosaurs; mammoths were mammals.
tryIt: Press a toy’s foot into play dough. Your print models a trace, not a real fossil.

questions.prompt: Which could be a fossil?
questions.explanation: A fossil can be a preserved trace, such as an ancient footprint.

questions.prompt: What do fossils help scientists learn about?
questions.explanation: Fossils are evidence of past living things and environments.

questions.prompt: Did humans live with non-bird dinosaurs such as Triceratops?
options: No, they lived at different times
questions.explanation: Non-bird dinosaurs died out millions of years before humans existed.

questions.prompt: Which animals are living dinosaurs?
questions.explanation: Birds belong to the dinosaur family tree.

questions.prompt: A woolly mammoth was what kind of animal?
questions.explanation: Mammoths were hairy relatives of elephants, not dinosaurs.

questions.prompt: Which scientist studies ancient life using fossils?
questions.explanation: Paleontologists study ancient life and its evidence.

questions.prompt: A fossil shell is found in rock high on a mountain. What might it show?
options: That rock formed in an old watery environment
questions.explanation: Places change over very long times. The rock may record an ancient sea.

questions.prompt: Which is evidence of how an ancient animal moved?
questions.explanation: A line of footprints can give clues about movement.

title: Map treasure
subject: Geography
description: Use directions to find your way.
lesson: A globe models Earth. A map shows a place on a flat surface.
A map key tells what symbols mean. A compass rose shows directions.
North, south, east, and west help us describe places. A map can show land and water.
tryIt: Make a map of one room. Add a key for a chair, a door, and a hidden paper star.

questions.prompt: What does a map key explain?
questions.explanation: A key, or legend, explains symbols and colors on a map.

questions.prompt: What is a globe a model of?
questions.explanation: A globe is a round model of Earth.

questions.prompt: Which direction is opposite north?
questions.explanation: North and south are opposite directions.

questions.prompt: Which direction is opposite east?
questions.explanation: East and west are opposite directions.

questions.prompt: What helps you find directions on a map?
questions.explanation: A compass rose labels directions.

questions.prompt: A blue shape is marked lake in the key. What does it show?
questions.explanation: Read the key to learn what each map symbol means.

questions.prompt: Which map would best help you find your classroom?
questions.explanation: Use a map of the place you need to explore.

questions.prompt: Why is a flat map useful?
options: It helps show where places are
It changes every ocean into land
questions.explanation: Maps help us find and compare locations.

title: Around Earth
subject: Geography
description: Meet seven continents and five oceans.
lesson: In our seven-continent model: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and Australia.
Countries are places with governments. A continent is a large land area. One continent can contain many countries.
Five named oceans connect around Earth: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Southern.
tryIt: On a globe, find North America, then trace across an ocean to another continent.

questions.prompt: Which continent contains the United States?
questions.explanation: The United States is in North America.

questions.prompt: Which continent contains China and India?
questions.explanation: China and India are countries in Asia.

questions.prompt: Which continent contains Brazil?
questions.explanation: Brazil is a country in South America.

questions.prompt: Which continent contains Kenya?
questions.explanation: Kenya is a country in Africa.

questions.prompt: Which continent is around the South Pole?
questions.explanation: Antarctica is an icy continent around the South Pole.

questions.prompt: Which is an ocean?
questions.explanation: The Pacific is an ocean; Virginia is a state and Brazil is a country.

questions.prompt: Which continent contains France?
questions.explanation: France is a country in Europe.

questions.prompt: Which is both a country and the name used for a continent?
questions.explanation: Australia is a country and a continent in the model used here. The wider region is called Oceania.

title: Country postcards
subject: Geography
lesson: A country is different from a continent. Many countries share one continent.
China and Japan are in Asia. Kenya and Egypt are in Africa. Brazil is in South America.
Mexico and Canada share North America with the United States. People in every country have many different lives.
tryIt: Choose a country on a globe. Tell a grown-up its continent and one thing you wonder about.

questions.prompt: Where is Japan?
questions.explanation: Japan is an island country in Asia.

questions.prompt: Which country is north of the main connected part of the United States?
questions.explanation: Canada is the northern neighbor of the contiguous United States.

questions.prompt: Which country is south of the United States and shares a border with it?
questions.explanation: Mexico and the United States share a border.

questions.prompt: Which country is in South America?
questions.explanation: Brazil is the largest country by area in South America.

questions.prompt: Which country is in Africa?
questions.explanation: Kenya is in eastern Africa.

questions.prompt: Which country is in Europe?
questions.explanation: Italy is a country in Europe.

questions.prompt: The Nile River runs through Egypt. Which continent is most of Egypt in?
questions.explanation: Most of Egypt is in Africa. Its Sinai Peninsula is in Asia.

questions.prompt: Which is a country rather than a continent?
questions.explanation: India is one of the countries in Asia.

title: Hello, neighbors!
subject: Geography
lesson: Culture includes languages, stories, music, food, art, and traditions. People within one country can have different cultures.
Some families celebrate Lunar New Year. Some celebrate Diwali. People choose different traditions, even in the same town.
Ask kindly instead of guessing about someone. We can enjoy differences and still share needs for care and friendship.
tryIt: Ask a grown-up about a family tradition. Draw it, then ask what a friend’s family enjoys.

questions.prompt: Which is part of culture?
questions.explanation: Culture includes many learned and shared ways of life.

questions.prompt: Do all people in one country follow the same traditions?
questions.explanation: Every country includes many kinds of people and traditions.

questions.prompt: What is a kind way to learn about a friend’s tradition?
options: Ask if they would like to tell you
questions.explanation: Ask respectfully, listen, and let people choose what to share.

questions.prompt: Some families celebrate Lunar New Year. Who celebrates it?
options: People in several countries and communities
Only one family in the world
questions.explanation: Lunar New Year traditions are celebrated in different ways in several cultures.

questions.prompt: Diwali is often called a festival of what?
questions.explanation: Many communities celebrate Diwali with light. Traditions and meanings vary.

questions.prompt: Which is true about languages?
options: One country can have many languages
Everyone speaks the same language at home
questions.explanation: Languages and countries do not match one to one.

questions.prompt: Which is a welcoming action?
options: Include a new child in a game
Say only your food is good
questions.explanation: Kindness helps people feel welcome. Learn how to say someone’s name.

questions.prompt: Can families share a tradition and celebrate it differently?
questions.explanation: Traditions can be shared and still vary from family to family.

title: Across America
subject: Geography
lesson: The United States is a country in North America. It has 50 states.
Washington, D.C., is the national capital. It is a federal district, not a state.
Alaska and Hawaii are states, too. The Atlantic is east of the mainland, and the Pacific is west.
tryIt: Find Virginia, Alaska, and Hawaii on a U.S. map. Notice that map boxes can move Alaska and Hawaii to fit.

questions.prompt: How many states are in the United States?
questions.explanation: The United States has 50 states.

questions.prompt: What is the national capital of the United States?
questions.explanation: Washington, D.C., is the national capital.

questions.prompt: Is Washington, D.C., one of the 50 states?
options: No, it is a federal district
questions.explanation: Washington, D.C., is a federal district separate from the states.

questions.prompt: Which ocean is east of Virginia?
questions.explanation: Virginia’s coast faces the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.prompt: Which ocean touches California’s coast?
questions.explanation: California is on the Pacific coast.

questions.prompt: Which state is a chain of islands in the Pacific?
questions.explanation: Hawaii is an island state in the Pacific Ocean.

questions.prompt: Which state lies northwest of Canada?
questions.explanation: Alaska is northwest of Canada and is a U.S. state.

questions.prompt: Virginia is part of which country?
questions.explanation: Virginia is one of the United States.

title: Hello, Virginia!
subject: Geography
lesson: Virginia is a U.S. state. Richmond is its capital.
Virginia has an Atlantic coast, the Chesapeake Bay, and the Blue Ridge Mountains.
Native peoples lived here long before English colonists arrived. Tribal communities are part of Virginia today.
tryIt: With a grown-up, find your town on a Virginia map. Look for one river or mountain nearby.

questions.prompt: What is Virginia’s capital?
questions.explanation: Richmond is the capital of Virginia.

questions.prompt: Which mountain range is in Virginia?
questions.explanation: The Blue Ridge Mountains cross part of Virginia.

questions.prompt: Which large bay touches Virginia?
questions.explanation: Chesapeake Bay borders part of Virginia and connects to the Atlantic.

questions.prompt: Which ocean is along Virginia’s eastern coast?
questions.explanation: The Atlantic Ocean lies along Virginia’s eastern coast.

questions.prompt: Which river flows through Richmond?
questions.explanation: The James River flows through Richmond.

questions.prompt: Which is a region of Virginia?
questions.explanation: Piedmont is one of Virginia’s five geographic regions.

questions.prompt: Were people living in Virginia before English colonists arrived?
questions.explanation: Native nations lived here long before the English colony. Native communities live here today.

questions.prompt: Which is true?
options: Virginia and West Virginia are different states
questions.explanation: Virginia and West Virginia are two different U.S. states.

title: Ice Age camp
subject: History
lesson: During the last glacial period, huge ice sheets covered parts of Earth. Not all of Earth was covered in ice.
Woolly mammoths were hairy relatives of elephants. Humans and mammoths lived at the same time.
Early people made tools, found food, and cared for one another. Scientists study objects and fossils to learn about them.
tryIt: Wrap two toy cups differently and imagine warm clothing. Ask how shelter and clothing help in cold places.

questions.prompt: Which animal lived during the last Ice Age?
questions.explanation: Woolly mammoths lived during the last glacial period.

questions.prompt: What covered parts of Earth during the last glacial period?
questions.explanation: Large ice sheets covered some regions, while other places had different climates.

questions.prompt: Was every place on Earth covered in ice?
questions.explanation: Ice covered parts of Earth, not the entire planet.

questions.prompt: Mammoths were related to which living animals?
questions.explanation: Mammoths and elephants belong to the same wider family.

questions.prompt: Did humans and mammoths live at the same time?
questions.explanation: There is evidence of humans and mammoths living at the same time.

questions.prompt: What could help people stay warm?
questions.explanation: People used knowledge, materials, and teamwork to survive cold conditions.

questions.prompt: Which gives evidence about early people?
options: A stone tool found by archaeologists
questions.explanation: Objects left behind can help archaeologists study past lives.

questions.prompt: Did people ride non-bird dinosaurs during the Ice Age?
questions.explanation: Non-bird dinosaurs had died out millions of years earlier.

title: First makers
subject: History
lesson: Prehistory means the time before written records in a place. It ended at different times in different places.
People made stone tools and art long before writing. They learned from one another.
Over time, some communities grew crops and kept animals. Farming and gathering did not change everywhere at once.
tryIt: Draw a story without words. Ask someone what clues helped them understand it.

questions.prompt: What does prehistory mean?
options: Time before written records in a place
questions.explanation: Prehistory is about written records, not about people being unimportant.

questions.prompt: Which could early people make from stone?
questions.explanation: People shaped stone into many useful tools.

questions.prompt: What can ancient art tell us?
questions.explanation: Art is one kind of evidence of how people expressed ideas.

questions.prompt: What is farming?
questions.explanation: Farming includes growing useful plants and caring for animals.

questions.prompt: Did farming begin in every place on the same day?
questions.explanation: Communities changed food practices at different times.

questions.prompt: What is an archaeologist likely to study?
questions.explanation: Archaeologists study evidence of people’s lives.

questions.prompt: Why was sharing knowledge useful?
questions.explanation: Sharing skills helped people solve problems together.

questions.prompt: Which came first?
questions.explanation: Stone tools were made long before electric technology.

title: River cities
subject: History
lesson: Ancient communities grew near rivers that supplied water. The Nile flows through Egypt.
Mesopotamia lay around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Some of its people wrote by pressing marks into clay.
Ancient Egypt used hieroglyphs. Farmers, builders, traders, and families all helped communities work.
tryIt: Make marks in play dough with a blunt stick. Invent a sign for water and one for food.

questions.prompt: Which river was important to ancient Egypt?
questions.explanation: The Nile supplied water and fertile land to ancient Egyptian communities.

questions.prompt: Why did many ancient communities grow near rivers?
questions.explanation: Rivers supported drinking, farming, travel, and trade.

questions.prompt: What are hieroglyphs?
questions.explanation: Hieroglyphs used signs to write language.

questions.prompt: Some people in Mesopotamia wrote on what?
questions.explanation: They pressed marks into clay tablets.

questions.prompt: Which rivers are linked with Mesopotamia?
questions.explanation: Mesopotamia was in the region of the Tigris and Euphrates.

questions.prompt: Who helped ancient cities work?
questions.explanation: Farmers, craftspeople, traders, and families all contributed.

questions.prompt: What could people trade?
questions.explanation: Trade let people exchange goods made or grown in different places.

questions.prompt: What is useful evidence about ancient writing?
questions.explanation: Surviving written objects are evidence historians can study.

title: Castle and town
subject: History
description: Meet farmers, builders, and book makers.
lesson: The Middle Ages is a name for a period of European history, roughly 500–1500 CE.
Many people farmed. Towns also had craftspeople and traders. Castles were fortified homes and strongholds.
Books could be copied by hand. While Europe had its Middle Ages, China and many other places had their own histories.
tryIt: Fold paper into a little book. Draw how a farmer, a builder, and a book maker help a town.

questions.prompt: The Middle Ages usually names a period in whose history?
questions.explanation: It is a period label used especially for European history, not a stage every culture followed.

questions.prompt: What did many people do for food?
questions.explanation: Farming supported many medieval communities.

questions.prompt: What was a castle built to help do?
questions.explanation: Castles were fortified buildings, often homes and defensive strongholds.

questions.prompt: Who might make pots, cloth, or tools?
questions.explanation: Craftspeople used skills to make useful objects.

questions.prompt: Before printing spread in Europe, how were many books copied?
questions.explanation: Copying a book by hand took time and skill.

questions.prompt: Were medieval towns home only to knights?
options: No, many kinds of people lived there
questions.explanation: Families, workers, traders, and many others lived in towns.

questions.prompt: Which two histories overlapped in time?
options: Europe’s Middle Ages and China’s Tang dynasty
Smartphones and the first stone tools
The Moon landing and ancient Egypt’s first pyramids
questions.explanation: Different places have histories happening at the same time.

questions.prompt: Which was useful to a medieval trader?
questions.explanation: Traders moved goods along roads and waterways.

title: China: Qin and Han
subject: History
lesson: A dynasty is a line of rulers, often from one family. Qin came before Han.
Qin rulers unified several states. The first Qin emperor’s tomb had a huge army of clay figures.
Han communities farmed, made goods, and traded. Routes now called the Silk Roads connected many places.
tryIt: Draw two time boxes: Qin, then Han. Add a clay figure to one and a trade route to the other.

questions.prompt: What is a dynasty?
options: A line of rulers, often from one family
questions.explanation: A dynasty is a succession of rulers often linked by family.

questions.prompt: Which came first?
questions.explanation: Qin came before Han in Chinese history.

questions.prompt: What were the famous Qin tomb soldiers made from?
questions.explanation: The terracotta figures were made of fired clay.

questions.prompt: What did Qin rulers bring together?
questions.explanation: Qin rulers unified states in what became an empire.

questions.prompt: What could travel along trade routes?
questions.explanation: Trade connected people, products, and ideas.

questions.prompt: Which was a real job during Han times?
questions.explanation: Farming and many crafts supported Han communities.

questions.prompt: Were the Silk Roads just one single road?
options: No, they were many connected routes
No, they were on the Moon
questions.explanation: The name refers to networks of routes across large regions.

questions.prompt: Which helps us study ancient China?
questions.explanation: Historians combine different kinds of evidence.

title: China: Tang to Ming
subject: History
lesson: Tang came before Song, and Ming came later. Other dynasties came between them, too.
Tang China had busy cities, poetry, and exchange with other places. Printing helped books spread during Tang and Song times.
Song craftspeople made fine ceramics. Many surviving sections of the Great Wall were built or rebuilt during Ming rule.
tryIt: Make a paper print by rubbing a crayon over a safe textured surface. Compare printing with drawing each mark again.

questions.prompt: Which of these dynasties came first?
questions.explanation: Tang was earlier than Song and Ming. There were also other dynasties.

questions.prompt: Which art was important in Tang China?
questions.explanation: Tang poets wrote works still read today.

questions.prompt: What did printing help people make?
questions.explanation: Printing helped reproduce writing and spread books.

questions.prompt: Ceramics are objects made mainly from what?
questions.explanation: Ceramics include pottery and porcelain made with clay and heat.

questions.prompt: Many standing Great Wall sections were built or rebuilt under which dynasty?
questions.explanation: Wall building happened over many periods; many well-known surviving sections are Ming.

questions.prompt: Were Qin, Han, Tang, Song, and Ming all the dynasties?
questions.explanation: These are a few selected dynasties, not the whole history of China.

questions.prompt: Which two existed at overlapping times?
options: Song China and Europe’s Middle Ages
Ming China and the first Moon landing
questions.explanation: Song history and part of Europe’s Middle Ages happened at the same time.

questions.prompt: What could visitors to a busy trade city exchange?
questions.explanation: Cities connected people from different places.

title: America’s first peoples
subject: History
description: Learn about Native nations, past and present.
lesson: Native peoples lived in the Americas long before European colonists arrived.
There were, and are, many distinct Native nations, languages, and ways of life. There is no single Native culture.
Native communities are here today. Many have their own governments and keep languages and traditions strong.
tryIt: With a grown-up, learn the name of a Native nation connected with your area from that nation’s own website.

questions.prompt: Who lived in the Americas before European colonists arrived?
questions.explanation: Many Native peoples had long histories in the Americas before colonization.

questions.prompt: Did every Native nation speak the same language?
questions.explanation: There were and are many distinct languages and nations.

questions.prompt: Are Native peoples part of life today?
questions.explanation: Native communities live, work, create, and govern today.

questions.prompt: Which is a respectful way to learn about a Native nation?
options: Listen to that nation’s own people
Treat every nation as the same
questions.explanation: Learn from Native voices and reliable sources.

questions.prompt: Could different Native communities have different homes and foods?
questions.explanation: Ways of life varied with places, resources, and traditions.

questions.prompt: Which crop was grown by many Native communities?
questions.explanation: Many Native farmers grew maize and other crops. Not every community farmed.

questions.prompt: Which is true about Native nations?
questions.explanation: Native nations have distinct histories and governments.

questions.prompt: Which sentence avoids a mistaken idea?
options: Native cultures are diverse and continue today
All Native people lived the same way
Native people exist only in the past
questions.explanation: We learn more accurately by recognizing both diversity and present-day life.

title: A new United States
subject: History
lesson: English colonists built Jamestown in Virginia in 1607 on land already home to Native peoples.
In 1776, thirteen colonies declared independence from Great Britain. The Constitution later set out a framework for government.
The promise of equal rights was not shared fairly. Enslaved people were denied freedom, and many people could not vote.
tryIt: Make three fair rules for a pretend club. Ask who should help decide the rules.

questions.prompt: Where was Jamestown established in 1607?
questions.explanation: English colonists established Jamestown in Virginia on Native peoples’ homeland.

questions.prompt: How many colonies declared independence in 1776?
questions.explanation: Thirteen colonies declared independence. The country later grew and changed.

questions.prompt: From which country did those colonies declare independence?
questions.explanation: The thirteen colonies declared independence from Great Britain.

questions.prompt: Which document announced independence?
questions.explanation: The Declaration announced the colonies’ decision in 1776.

questions.prompt: Which document sets out the U.S. government’s framework?
questions.explanation: The Constitution describes how the national government is organized.

questions.prompt: Did everyone have equal rights at the founding?
questions.explanation: Many people were denied freedom, voting rights, and fair treatment.

questions.prompt: Was Virginia empty before colonists arrived?
questions.explanation: Native nations had communities and histories there already.

questions.prompt: What is a fair rule for a club?
options: Only one child may speak forever
questions.explanation: Thinking about fair rules helps us discuss government and rights.

title: Meet past presidents
subject: History
lesson: A U.S. president is an elected leader, not a king. Presidents must follow the Constitution.
George Washington was the first president. Thomas Jefferson was the third. Abraham Lincoln was president during the Civil War.
Leaders can do important things and also cause harm. Washington and Jefferson enslaved people; a complete history includes those people’s lives.
tryIt: Draw a good leader listening to other people. Tell a grown-up why listening matters.

questions.prompt: Who was the first U.S. president?
questions.explanation: George Washington became the first U.S. president in 1789.

questions.prompt: Who was the third U.S. president?
questions.explanation: Thomas Jefferson served after Washington and John Adams.

questions.prompt: Who was president during the American Civil War?
questions.explanation: Lincoln was president during the Civil War.

questions.prompt: Is the U.S. president a king?
questions.explanation: The president is an elected leader with powers limited by the Constitution.

questions.prompt: Who else helps make national laws?
questions.explanation: Congress makes laws. The president has a different role in the government.

questions.prompt: Where does the U.S. president live and work?
questions.explanation: The White House is in Washington, D.C.

questions.prompt: Should presidents follow the Constitution?
questions.explanation: The Constitution limits the powers of government.

questions.prompt: Why learn about people harmed by past leaders, too?
questions.explanation: History includes leaders’ actions and the lives of the people those actions affected.

title: Working for fairness
subject: History
description: Meet people who worked for freedom.
lesson: Slavery treated people as property and denied their freedom. It was wrong. Enslaved people resisted and sought freedom.
Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and helped others escape. The Underground Railroad was a network of people and routes, not a subway.
The 13th Amendment ended legal slavery, except as punishment for crime. Later, civil rights activists kept working against unfair laws and treatment.
tryIt: Name one way to make a game fairer. Talk with a grown-up about what to do when a rule is unfair.

questions.prompt: What did slavery deny people?
questions.explanation: Slavery denied people freedom and treated them as property. It was wrong.

questions.prompt: What did Harriet Tubman help people do?
questions.explanation: After escaping slavery, Tubman returned to help other people reach freedom.

questions.prompt: Was the Underground Railroad a real train line?
options: No, it was a network helping people escape
questions.explanation: People used routes and safe places. The name was a code, not an actual railroad.

questions.prompt: What did the 13th Amendment do?
options: End legal slavery, with a punishment-for-crime exception
questions.explanation: The amendment abolished slavery except as punishment for crime after conviction.

questions.prompt: Did ending slavery immediately end all unfair treatment?
questions.explanation: People continued fighting racism and unequal treatment.

questions.prompt: What did civil rights activists work for?
questions.explanation: Civil rights activism challenges unfair laws and discrimination.

questions.prompt: Were enslaved people part of the struggle for freedom?
options: Yes, they resisted and acted for freedom
questions.explanation: Enslaved and formerly enslaved people were central to the fight for freedom.

questions.prompt: What helps us learn a fuller history?
questions.explanation: Historical evidence includes the experiences of many people.

title: 50-state trail
subject: Geography
description: Learn a few states at a time.
lesson: Each of the 50 states has a capital, where its state government works.
A state capital is not always the largest city. Richmond is Virginia’s capital; Washington, D.C., is the national capital.
Explore the cards first. It is fine to learn just a few today.
tryIt: Pick three state cards. Find those states on a U.S. map with a grown-up.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Alabama?
questions.explanation: Montgomery is the capital of Alabama. A state capital is a center of state government.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Alaska?
questions.explanation: Juneau is the capital of Alaska. A state capital is a center of state government.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Arizona?
